content: Endometriosis is a common gynecological condition that can significantly impact the quality of life of affected women. Its clinical manifestations range from being completely asymptomatic to causing chronic pelvic pain, with dysmenorrhea being the most prominent symptom. Current approaches to managing pain associated with endometriosis are insufficient. Acupuncture has been explored as a treatment option for various gynecological conditions, but its efficacy in alleviating pain specifically related to endometriosis remains uncertain. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of acupuncture in managing pain caused by endometriosis. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Menstrual Disorders and Subfertility Group (MSDG) Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, AMED, PsycINFO, CNKI, and TCMDS, covering studies from their inception up to 2010. Additionally, reference lists of relevant articles were reviewed. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized singleor double-blind controlled trials involving women of reproductive age with laparoscopically confirmed endometriosis. These trials compared acupuncture (whether body, scalp, or auricular) to placebo, sham treatments, no treatment, conventional therapies, or Chinese herbal medicine. Three independent reviewers assessed the risk of bias and extracted data from the studies. Authors of the included studies were contacted for additional information. However, meta-analyses could not be performed because only one study met the inclusion criteria. The primary outcome of interest was the reduction in pain associated with endometriosis. Secondary outcomes included improvements in quality of life, pregnancy rates, adverse effects, and recurrence rates of endometriosis. Out of 24 studies identified, only one trial, involving 67 participants, met all the inclusion criteria. This trial measured pain scores and cure rates using the Guideline for Clinical Research on New Chinese Medicine. The results showed that dysmenorrhea scores were significantly lower in the acupuncture group compared to the control group, with a mean difference of -4.81 points (95% confidence interval: -6.25 to -3.37, P < 0.00001) on a 15-point scale. The total effective rate, defined as the proportion of participants classified as cured, significantly effective, or effective, was 91.9% for auricular acupuncture and 60% for Chinese herbal medicine (risk ratio: 3.04, 95% confidence interval: 1.65 to 5.62, P = 0.0004). While there was no significant difference in improvement rates between auricular acupuncture and Chinese herbal medicine for mild to moderate dysmenorrhea, auricular acupuncture was found to significantly reduce pain in cases of severe dysmenorrhea. Unfortunately, data on secondary outcomes were not available. The authors concluded that the evidence supporting the effectiveness of acupuncture for pain management in endometriosis is limited, as it is based on the findings of a single study. This underscores the urgent need for future research involving well-designed, double-blinded, randomized controlled trials to evaluate the efficacy of various types of acupuncture in comparison to conventional therapies.
